doc_summary: Marks proposes 'cognition-based oversight' and a model problem (Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers) that assumes behavioral evaluation cannot separate good from bad models, and presents SHIFT as a proof-of-concept. The post is relevant to eval design because it treats behavioral evidence as insufficient against situationally-aware schemers and argues for inspecting internal cognition instead.

items.claim: Prefers evaluating models by whether they perform intended cognition over judging input/output behavior, because behavior alone may be unable to separate good models from bad ones that are trying to look good.
items.quote: In brief, cognition-based oversight aims to evaluate models according to whether they’re performing intended cognition, instead of whether they have intended input/output behavior.

items.claim: Distrusts behavioral evidence from setups where the model can detect scrutiny, since situationally-aware schemers behave well only when they think bad behavior would be caught.
items.quote: **Situationally-aware schemers** behave well only when they think bad behavior would be caught. [For example](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06942), a scheming code generation model might write vulnerability-free code only when it expects the code to be closely audited, but otherwise insert subtle backdoors.

items.claim: Distrusts reward signals like human approval as proof of good behavior, because sycophantic reward hackers score highly while doing the wrong thing, such as tampering with the camera instead of preventing theft.
items.quote: **Sycophantic reward hackers** take actions that look good to the overseer, even when this conflicts with doing what the overseer actually wants.

items.claim: Prefers testing under a deliberately pessimistic assumption (behaviorally identical models) over improving existing behavioral oversight, because it forces attention onto the hardest part of the problem.
items.quote: Instead of asking how to improve the existing approaches to scalable oversight, I’m going to take a different tack: **I will impose the pessimistic assumption that our models are effectively** ***behaviorally identical***

items.claim: Prefers a simplified, crisp model problem (classifiers with exactly identical outputs) over realistic general agents, as long as it keeps most of the technical difficulty and removes assumptions that are hard to pin down.
items.quote: The point of DBIC – introduced in the next section – is to simplify by moving to a classification setting where we *can* assume exactly identical model outputs, thus removing the need for tricky-to-pin-down assumptions that limit overseer judgment.

items.claim: Treats a result as convincing when it matches an oracle or ground truth that the method was not given access to, and flags 'skyline' conditions that cheat with held-out data.
items.quote: This is as good as possible: it matches the performance of an oracle classifier trained directly on balanced data.

items.claim: Anticipates where a method will fail by working through the hard case (ELK), and notes that interpretability can just reduce one hard problem to an equally hard one.
items.quote: I think there’s a good chance that this approach will reduce the problem of discriminating $C_g$ vs. $C_b$ to an equally-difficult problem of discriminating desired vs. undesired features.

items.claim: Chooses what to test by looking for leveraged settings where the interpretability task is easy but the behavioral task is intractable, maximizing risk reduction per unit of difficulty.
items.quote: identifying problem settings where cognition-based-oversight gives us an especially good *bang-for-our-buck* where “our buck” = “interpretability difficulty” and “bang” = “reduction in AI existential risk.”

items.claim: Is careful to separate in-principle counterexamples from empirical claims, saying the failure modes need not have occurred or be likely.
items.quote: To be clear, I’m not claiming that these examples have empirically come up, or that they are likely to arise

items.claim: Proposes using interpretability to set state of the art on a measurement-tampering benchmark as a field-level test, with failure there a bad sign for interpretability.
items.quote: If our interpretability tools can’t do this, then I’m worried they’ll struggle to prove useful in other settings.

items.claim: Proposes functional interpretations of features, understanding them through their roles in circuits rather than in isolation, since inspecting input/output behavior is unsatisfying for cognition-based oversight.
items.quote: My best guess for a path forward here is *functional interpretations of features*. By this I mean: understanding features in terms of the roles they play in circuits, rather than in isolation.
